I am acting as the implementor.I will read the spec, public tests, and prior findings. Then I will draft the implementation plan and point-by-point rebuttal.I will draft a complete implementation plan for the walcodec package.

No prior adversary findings exist. I will draft the plan to plan/plan.md and omit any rebuttal. The plan will cover the public API, internal data model, rule satisfaction, test approach, and edge cases.

I am beginning to draft the public API. I will ensure the plan is complete and robust against adversarial scrutiny.

The public API is now defined. A Record interface with Kind() uint8 distinguishes Put and Delete variants. Encode and Decode functions will handle byte slices. A corrupt stream error is exported. The wire format uses version 1 frames with a CRC32-IEEE checksum over type and payload.

Frame length is capped at 16 MiB. Any frame exceeding this limit is rejected as corrupt before any allocation.

Put payloads contain a key length prefix, the key bytes, a value length prefix, and the value bytes. Delete payloads contain only a key length prefix and the key bytes.

A nil or empty Value both encode to a zero-length value field and decode back to an empty slice. They are treated as equal.

The version byte is validated before any frames are read. An unknown version triggers ErrCorrupt.

Decode will reject frames with mismatched CRCs, unknown type tags, truncated data, or lengths exceeding the cap. It must round-trip Encode output exactly and preserve stream order. Duplicate keys are kept in their original order.

An empty record slice encodes to a one-byte version-only stream that decodes back to an empty slice without error. Decode called on nil or zero-length input returns ErrCorrupt.

The frame length field counts only the type byte plus payload bytes. A zero length therefore implies no type byte exists.

The minimum valid frame length is one byte, covering only the type tag. Before allocating any buffer, the decoder must verify that the claimed length is at least one byte and that the stream contains enough bytes to cover both the payload and the trailing CRC.

The public test for oversized frames only asserts the error, yet the spec requires rejecting before any allocation. I am also weighing whether unknown type tags should be checked after CRC or before.

I have settled on a deterministic decode order. The decoder will first verify the version byte, then read each frame's length prefix, check that it is within the 16 MiB cap and not truncated, read the type tag and payload, verify the CRC, and finally reject unknown type tags. This sequence ensures every invalid frame returns ErrCorrupt regardless of whether the cause is a bad CRC or an unrecognized type.

I am refining the decode sequence. After reading the length prefix, the decoder will verify that the stream contains at least len+4 bytes before allocating any buffer. A zero-length frame is treated as corrupt because it lacks a type byte. The parser will strictly enforce that payloads contain no trailing bytes and that internal length prefixes match the actual payload size.

I am finalizing the strict payload parsing rules. A well-formed payload must consume every byte claimed by its length prefixes; any trailing bytes or missing bytes are treated as corrupt. I am also noting that Go strings are arbitrary bytes, so key encoding should write raw string bytes without assuming UTF-8.

Decoding will reconstruct Go strings from raw bytes without UTF-8 validation.

Payload length is bounded by the 16 MiB cap, so it fits safely in an int. Key and value length prefixes are uint32, which can exceed the payload size. The decoder must verify that klen and vlen do not exceed the remaining payload bytes before allocating any string or slice.

Encode will return a distinct non-Corrupt error when given an unknown Record type or a nil interface in the slice. The spec does not define this error, so the plan should use an idiomatic Go error such as `fmt.Errorf("walcodec: unknown record type %T", rec)`.

Encode must reject records whose type and payload exceed 16 MiB. This prevents writing frames that Decode would reject.

Key and value lengths are uint32, so Encode must return an error when a Go string exceeds math.MaxUint32 bytes.

The total frame size must also stay within the 16 MiB cap.

I will decode empty values as non-nil `[]byte{}` slices. This satisfies the spec's requirement that both nil and empty inputs produce a length-0 slice, and it avoids unnecessary allocations.

The decoder will copy payload bytes into fresh slices rather than aliasing the input buffer. This prevents caller mutations from corrupting the underlying stream and ensures exact round-trip semantics.

The plan will explicitly require copying key and value bytes into fresh slices so decoded records do not alias the input buffer. For an empty stream, Decode will return a nil or empty slice with length zero and no error.

The decoder will accumulate records in a nil slice and grow it with append. This stays nil when no records are present and passes the public test.

After validating the version byte, the decoder will not attempt to parse any frames if the version is invalid.

It will process multiple frames sequentially until the input buffer is fully consumed. Any remaining bytes that are fewer than a full frame header are treated as a truncated stream.

The CRC32-IEEE checksum covers only the type tag and payload bytes. It excludes the length prefix.

All uint32 fields will be encoded in big-endian byte order. The Record interface will use value receivers for Kind so that both Put and *Put satisfy the interface.

The frame length formula is `1 + 4 + len(key) + 4 + len(value)` for Put records and `1 + 4 + len(key)` for Delete records. Encode must check that the sum does not exceed the 16 MiB cap, and it must reject keys or values longer than `math.MaxUint32` before any allocation.

The API is one-shot: []byte in, []byte out. Encode will use a growable slice or bytes.Buffer for output. Decode will not allocate key or value buffers until the length prefixes are verified against the remaining payload.

The decoder will slice the input buffer directly for the frame payload without copying. CRC32-IEEE can be computed over that existing slice. This avoids allocating a new buffer for every frame.

The encoder will always write the version byte 0x01 first. The decoder will check the CRC before validating the type tag, so a corrupted type byte is treated as corrupt rather than as an unknown record.

The decoder will not deduplicate keys; it will append every record in order. Empty keys are valid and must round-trip correctly. The encoder will write raw bytes for keys without UTF-8 validation, since Go strings may contain any byte values. Public tests check for ErrCorrupt using errors.Is, so the plan should ensure the error is wrapped or defined as a named constant.

ErrCorrupt will be returned directly without wrapping, since errors.Is still matches a bare sentinel. Encode will only return an error for size overflows; normal valid records must not fail.

The encoder will return a distinct non-sentinel error for records that exceed the 16 MiB frame cap, since the spec only defines ErrCorrupt. Decode will store Put and Delete values directly in the returned slice rather than pointers, because public tests type-assert against the value types.

The package will be named `walcodec` at module root with Go 1.25. The plan will place types, constants, and errors in `walcodec.go`.

The implementation will be split into `record.go` and `codec.go` for clarity. The frame cap constant is 16777216 bytes, so a length of exactly that value is valid while any larger length is corrupt.

The plan will describe additional internal tests to cover edge cases the public suite misses. No implementation or test files will be written now.

The plan will add internal tests for the empty-stream case, unknown version bytes, and exact-frame-capacity boundaries. A test for a length that exceeds the cap by one byte without allocating a 16 MiB buffer is also noted.

The plan will also cover truncated streams cut at the version byte, length prefix, type tag, payload, or CRC. It will test CRC corruption at any byte position and trailing junk after a valid frame that is not a complete frame. Extra bytes inside a payload and key or value lengths exceeding their remaining bounds are included. The spec does not define whether Decode must be atomic across multiple frames.

The plan will explicitly require that Decode returns nil records and ErrCorrupt whenever any frame is corrupt, with no partial results. Additional tests will cover empty keys, binary keys containing NUL or non-UTF-8 bytes, values with embedded zeros, Delete-then-Put ordering, and Encode rejecting unsupported types or nil records.

Nil and empty values must encode to identical bytes because both produce a zero-length value field. A valid CRC on a truncated payload or extra trailing bytes inside the payload must be rejected as corrupt. The decoder must validate the version byte before parsing any frame length, so an invalid version is reported immediately rather than misattributed to a size overflow.

The implementation will be pure functions with no persistent state. Wire constants remain unexported, and the decoder will not use maps or deduplication.

The encoder will compute the CRC32-IEEE checksum over the type tag and payload bytes, then compare it with the stored four-byte CRC in big-endian order. For each record, it writes the frame length prefix, the type byte, key length, key bytes, value length, value bytes, and finally the computed CRC. Nil and empty values both produce zero-length payloads and require no value bytes. The encoder may optionally pre-size its output buffer by summing the exact byte lengths of all records first, though overflow checks are required.

The encoder will append to a slice starting with the version byte. It will check frame size limits before writing each record so no corrupt frames are emitted. The functions are stateless and safe for concurrent use.

Encode will return a one-byte slice containing only the version byte when given an empty record slice. The public tests verify that the result has length one.

The Encode function will accept both value and pointer receivers for Put, Delete, and nil records. This is more idiomatic than requiring only values, and it does not violate the specification.

The Kind method will use a value receiver. A nil pointer to Put or Delete would panic if called through an interface, so the encoder must reject nil records before invoking it.

The encoder will dispatch on record type via a type switch rather than calling Kind(), because Kind() with a value receiver panics on nil pointers. Kind() remains for the interface contract. The frame length prefix covers the type tag plus payload, and Decode will slice the buffer to that exact length before parsing.

The decoder will validate frame lengths by reading the prefix as a 32-bit unsigned integer, rejecting any value above the 16 MiB cap. It will then check that the remaining buffer is large enough to hold the full frame including its CRC.

For key and value lengths inside the payload, the decoder will verify that the length field is non-negative and does not exceed the remaining payload size. On 32-bit systems, casting a key or value length to int could overflow if the field exceeds MaxInt32, so the plan must guard against that.

The decoder will guard key and value lengths by comparing them as uint64 against the remaining payload size, then safely cast to int because the payload itself is capped at 16 MiB minus one byte. Values will be copied with bytes.Clone so decoded records do not alias the input buffer.

The decoder will use `make([]byte, vlen)` and `copy` to build values, rather than `bytes.Clone`, because `bytes.Clone(nil)` returns nil while `make` always yields a non-nil slice. This ensures both nil and empty inputs decode to the same non-nil length-zero value.

The spec requires nil and empty values to encode to identical bytes, so the public tests must compare encoded output rather than decoded records.

The plan will explicitly require that Encode(Put{Value:nil}) and Encode(Put{Value:[]byte{}}) produce identical bytes. It will also state that Decode rejects unknown version bytes, rejects extra data after valid frames, and never allocates a buffer larger than the frame cap.

The decoder will read frame lengths directly from four-byte slices with `encoding/binary.BigEndian.Uint32` to avoid reflection and accidental large allocations. Multiple records in a single `Encode` call will be emitted as sequential frames with no separators. Kind values are fixed at 1 and 2 for version 1, and exported types and functions will include idiomatic Go documentation comments.

The plan will not modify the existing public test file. The implementation will be placed in additional .go files within the same module root.

The plan will explicitly reject frames with length zero or less than one as corrupt, because the frame format requires a positive type byte. It will also verify that the payload length matches the exact expected size for Put and Delete records, rejecting any frame whose length implies an incorrect payload length.

The decoder must validate the version byte before parsing any frame length, including before checking for oversized frames. The 16 MiB cap is strictly greater than 16<<20. Returned records are concrete values rather than pointers to satisfy the public test type switches. Duplicate keys are preserved and maps are not used.

The public test file explicitly avoids asserting the written version byte is 1, so a v2 decoder can still accept v1 fixtures. The v1 implementation must therefore emit version 1 as required by the specification.

The CRC covers only the type tag and payload bytes, excluding the frame length prefix. A decoder must reject unknown record types such as type 99 even when the payload is empty. The implementation will copy value bytes into fresh slices to prevent aliasing with the input buffer.

The plan will specify the exact error type returned when Encode receives an invalid record. A valid CRC over malformed payload bytes must still be rejected as corrupt, because structural validation is separate from checksum verification. No whitespace or UTF-8 validation is required.

A Delete frame whose payload exceeds 4 plus the key length will be rejected as trailing junk. A Put frame missing its value length field will also be treated as corrupt. Offset arithmetic will use careful checks to avoid integer overflow. If a frame claims to fit within the buffer but the bytes are truncated, the decoder will return ErrCorrupt without allocating a large slice. After the final frame, no leftover bytes are allowed; success is only reached when the stream ends exactly at the last byte.

The decoder will verify the CRC before checking the record type, so a bad CRC on an unknown type still returns ErrCorrupt. The maximum key length for Delete frames is 16777211 bytes.

The maximum combined key and value length for Put frames is 16777207 bytes. Decode must never panic on any input because every access is bounds-checked. Encode must not panic when given a nil Value. The plan will include compile-time interface assertions that Put and Delete satisfy the Record interface.

The exact error string for ErrCorrupt will be "walcodec: corrupt stream" to match the specification. The implementation will use only standard library imports and avoid any import cycles. A Put frame with a zero-length value but a non-zero key is valid.

The phrase "not read" means the decoder must not consume or access the frame body bytes when a length exceeds the 16 MiB cap. It returns ErrCorrupt immediately after reading the length prefix, without slicing or copying the payload. If a frame is both oversized and truncated, it still returns ErrCorrupt.

The decoder will return only ErrCorrupt for decode failures. It will not wrap errors or return io.ErrUnexpectedEOF, because the public tests rely on errors.Is and direct equality checks.

The plan will specify that Encode(nil) and Encode([]Record{}) both produce the same empty-frame bytes. The implementation will be placed in the worktree directory when coding begins.

The plan will describe the test strategy without adding new test files. It will note that `go test ./...` and `go vet ./...` will run from the worktree, and that extra edge-case tests may be added during implementation.

No prior findings file exists, so no point-by-point rebuttal is needed. The plan will strictly implement version 1 as specified, without introducing v2 concerns.

The plan will be comprehensive and precise. Encode must return an error for records that exceed the 16 MiB cap or use an unknown record type, because the function signature already includes an error return.

The plan will also reject keys whose length exceeds the maximum uint32 value, returning an error even though practical memory limits make this unlikely. A helper function will compute frame body lengths by summing type tag, key length, and payload bytes, with explicit overflow checks to prevent wrap-around.

The plan will include a concrete Decode algorithm sketch that consumes the version byte first, then iterates over frames with a decodeFrame helper. Encode will be described with an exact step-by-step algorithm to eliminate ambiguity.

The `decodeFrame` helper will read the four-byte length prefix with `binary.BigEndian.Uint32`, reject any frame whose declared length exceeds the 16 MiB cap or is less than one, and verify that the total frame size fits within the input buffer before subslicing to extract the type tag and payload. The CRC is then read from the final four bytes of the frame.

The decoder will verify the CRC against the full body bytes before parsing the type tag. A Put record is decoded by reading a length-prefixed string for the key, then a length-prefixed byte slice for the value, and rejecting any trailing bytes. The decoder will use a `readLPBytes` helper that reads a four-byte big-endian length prefix.

The decoder will use a `readLPBytes` helper that rejects truncated payloads before allocating any slice, returning a non-nil empty byte slice for zero-length values. A `readLPString` helper will perform the same bounds check and copy the bytes into a string. Empty keys decode to `""`, and nil values decode to `[]byte{}` so that `bytes.Equal(nil, []byte{})` is true, satisfying the equality checks in the public tests.

The plan will document that a decoded value of length zero must be a non-nil empty slice, not nil. Preserving nil would make the slice header distinguishable, but the specification treats nil and empty as equivalent and the public tests rely on bytes.Equal.

The stream must preserve record order exactly as the input slice indexes them. No compression, whole-stream checksum, or multi-version support is required.

The plan will omit any intermediate AST or stored frame struct, keeping the internal data model minimal with only exported Record types and unexported size constants. It will also include a rule-by-rule mapping table that links each specification bullet to its implementation mechanism.

The plan will map the nine public tests to implementation mechanisms and note private tests. It will include the worktree path for the implementor. No point-by-point rebuttal is needed because no prior findings file exists.

The plan will explicitly state that Encode failures return a distinct non-nil error with the `walcodec:` prefix, never ErrCorrupt. Decode failures must be exactly ErrCorrupt, not wrapped. On any failure, the first return value is nil.

The round-trip rule implies Encode must not emit frames larger than the 16 MiB cap, because Decode would reject them. Encode must return an error for records that exceed the limit. Encode also cannot write unknown Record types, since only known tags are defined.

Encode must return an error when given a nil interface element, because calling methods on a nil interface would panic. A version-only stream is encoded as a single byte `1`, and Decode returns a nil slice with length zero.

The plan will explicitly state that Decode returns a nil slice with length zero and no error for a version-only stream. The public test only checks that the result has length zero, so this satisfies the specification.

The plan will return a non-nil empty slice `[]Record{}` for a version-only stream. This matches the specification's literal wording "an empty slice" more tightly than a nil slice.

The CRC will use the IEEE polynomial via `hash/crc32.ChecksumIEEE`, not Castagnoli. All length prefixes, key lengths, value lengths, and CRCs are big-endian. Keys are raw Go string bytes with no UTF-8 validation or null termination.

Value bytes are copied during decode and encode so the result does not alias the input. Decode panics on no input and Encode panics on nil records, nil elements, or unknown types. The package is safe for concurrent use with no mutable state. The 16 MiB cap is defined as a constant and equal-length frames are accepted.

The decoder will reject truncated frames at specific boundaries: a version byte with fewer than three length bytes, a length prefix with an incomplete body, a CRC with fewer than four bytes, or a payload length prefix that exceeds the remaining buffer. It will also reject any frame whose key or value length exceeds the available payload.

The 16 MiB cap is checked immediately after reading the uint32 length prefix, before any truncation check and before allocating slices. An unknown version byte is rejected before reading any length field.

The decoder will verify the CRC before checking the type tag, so an unknown tag with a valid CRC is rejected as ErrCorrupt. A byte-level worked example for a Put record will be included to eliminate ambiguity.

The plan will include a concrete byte-level worked example for a Put record, showing the exact sequence of key length, key bytes, value length, and value bytes within the frame body. It will also define a `Record` interface with a `Kind() uint8` method, and implement `Kind()` on both `Put` and `Delete` to return 1 and 2 respectively.

Encode will use a type switch on the concrete record type rather than calling Kind(), because only Put and Delete carry the required Key and Value fields. A custom type that returns an existing kind but is not a known record would be rejected as unknown. Encode will also accept pointer values such as *Put and *Delete by dereferencing them, returning an error for nil pointers to avoid panics.

The plan will type-switch directly on `Put` and `Delete` values only. Pointer handling is omitted to keep the API simple and avoid unspecified behavior.

The implementation will be split into `record.go`, `encode.go`, and `decode.go`. The existing public test file will not be modified. The `go.mod` file will remain unchanged, and exported API comments will be included.

The decoder must read the four-byte length prefix to detect an oversized frame, but it will not read the payload bytes that follow. Decode may allocate a result slice for valid records, yet the oversize short-circuit returns before any frame allocation occurs.

The cap check must precede any arithmetic on the length prefix to avoid overflow. A frame with a 16 MiB plus one byte body and a 0xFFFFFFFF length prefix are both rejected before any allocation.

Decode will return a single error for the entire stream. If any frame has a bad CRC, the first valid record is discarded and only ErrCorrupt is returned. Returning partial results alongside an error would violate the all-or-nothing contract.

The decoder will reject any stream that ends with truncated bytes after a valid frame. Encode will emit only the version byte when given an empty slice. The implementation will accept only version 1 and reject versions 0 and 2.

The plan will not use runtime memory statistics to prove that no allocation occurs before the cap check. Instead, it will rely on the code structure: only a length prefix read and a Uint32 load happen before the comparison. A unit test will feed a short buffer with a huge length prefix and expect ErrCorrupt.

An optional boundary test will construct a legal frame with a payload exactly at the 16 MiB limit and expect success. This allocates roughly 16 MiB once, so it is slow but valid. The public suite will rely on the existing oversize test to exercise the cap logic.

The exact 16 MiB boundary will be tested by encoding a record whose frame body is exactly 16<<20 bytes and decoding it back. A Delete frame with a key length of 16777211 bytes yields a body of exactly 16 MiB, requiring roughly 16 MiB of allocation. This test locks the off-by-one cap check.

The exact 16 MiB boundary test is sufficient; no additional cap-exceeding test is needed. A buffer that is long enough to tempt a naive reader but still rejects the oversized length prefix is acceptable. The public suite already exercises this path. The plan will also include tests for a crafted frame with a correct CRC but an unknown type tag, and for a valid frame whose payload contains trailing bytes after the expected end.

The plan will also test concatenated valid frames, high bytes in keys, empty keys, and nil versus empty values. It will assert that Decode does not retain an alias to the input buffer.

A test will mutate a decoded value and re-decode the original buffer to prove that Decode does not alias its input. Encode will reject unknown record types by checking that errors.Is(err, ErrCorrupt) or that the error is non-nil. go vet issues are expected to be minimal.

The implementation must avoid naming collisions with the public test helpers `beU32`, `mkFrame`, `recEq`, and `recsEq` because the tests live in the same package. Unexported helpers should use different names such as `putU32`, `appendU32`, and `frameLen`.

Encode will call `Kind()` to determine the frame type tag, keeping a single source of truth for the mapping between record types and tags. A compile-time assertion in `record.go` will ensure both `Put` and `Delete` implement the `Record` interface.

ErrCorrupt must be a package-level variable, not a constant, because errors.New returns an error interface. The plan is being written to be precise enough that an implementor can follow it blindly without ambiguity. Specific off-by-one risks are being enumerated and pinned down, including the exact cap comparison and the frame length formula.

A frame with length zero is derived as corrupt because the payload length underflows. The decoder will use uint64 arithmetic to prevent overflow when summing key and value lengths against remaining bytes.

The decoder will consume the frame body sequentially rather than adding untrusted lengths in uint32, preventing overflow. Go's string([]byte) conversion always copies, so no aliasing risk exists. A partial frame immediately after the version byte is rejected as corrupt. The decoder may append records incrementally and discard the slice on failure; this avoids user-visible partial results.

The spec's "before any allocation" rule applies to the oversized frame itself, not to the entire Decode call. If an oversized frame appears after valid frames, the decoder may have already allocated buffers for those earlier records; it will discard them and return only ErrCorrupt.

The API accepts a []byte slice, so the decoder must not allocate a new buffer of size len and must not un-read the caller’s input. Encode emits records in first-to-last order. The CRC is big-endian on the wire, matching the public test helper.

The decoder will reject frames with type tags 0, 255, or any value outside the known range as corrupt. Duplicate detection must not use a map; it is simply an append-only log where every record is preserved in order. The Record interface and its Key and Value fields are exported.

Value is a []byte, not a string. Encode must return a one-byte slice containing version 1 and a nil error for empty input; returning nil would fail the length check. An internal test will assert that the version byte is exactly 1, since the spec requires it.

A test will flip the version byte to 2 on valid encoded output and expect ErrCorrupt. The 16 MiB limit is confirmed as exactly 16777216.

The 16 MiB cap applies only to the `len` field, not to the full frame. The payload maximum is therefore 16777215 bytes. Encode must set the length prefix exactly to the size of the type tag plus the payload, with no padding allowed.

Encode and Decode are inverses for all values Encode accepts. Decode returns ErrCorrupt for any bytes that Encode would never produce, including trailing junk, bad CRC, unknown type, bad version, truncation, oversize, and inconsistent length prefixes. Encoding a decoded record yields the same bytes as the original encoding.

Canonical encoding will use vlen 0 for zero-length values and omit the value field on Delete frames. Put always writes a vlen prefix even when it is zero. The implementation will target Go 1.25 but use only basic language features; make([]byte, n) is preferred over bytes.Clone for clarity.

The plan will list concrete helper signatures: `appendU32`, `encodeRecord`, `decodeFrame`, `decodePutPayload`, `decodeDeletePayload`, and `readU32Prefix`. Key strings are read with `string(b[:n])` after bounds checks. The helper `beU32` is avoided to prevent naming collisions with the public test suite.

Unexported error variables `errUnsupported` and `errTooLarge` will be used internally. The package tests can reference them directly because they live in the same package.

The plan will explicitly state that Encode returns a distinct internal error for oversized records rather than ErrCorrupt. ErrCorrupt is reserved for corrupt Decode inputs, so using it for an oversized Encode would mislead callers into thinking the stream itself is invalid.

The plan will use a single internal error for nil records, nil pointers, and unknown types. CRC verification will use `crc32.ChecksumIEEE` directly to avoid ambiguity about initialization values. The decoder will compare CRCs with `!=` on uint32 rather than `bytes.Equal`, and timing-safe comparison is not required.
